subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the house will permit me, in the Prime Minister's name, to do something which is rather unusual, about a man who was certainly unusual. I refer to the death of which we learned, in some cases, just a few moments ago, of Lord Beaverbrook who, like many a native of Ontario, was perhaps rather more attached to another part of Canada than to his native province, but whose attachment to Canada throughout his long and remarkable life gives us a reason for referring to his death after that long and very full life.
All of us recall, either in our own experience or as students of what has happened in the past, the great services Lord Beaverbrook rendered to the cause of his adopted country, to the cause of his native country and to the cause of freedom in two world wars.
We also acknowledge that he was one of the foremost native sons of our country, and I am sure we would all wish to express our sympathy to Lady Beaverbrook and all members of the Aitken family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
The
death of Lord Beaverbrook will come as a great shock to all Canadians, but especially to those of us who live in the province of New Brunswick. Lord Beaverbrook was one of four men who came from that little province and who made their mark-Bonar Law, R. B. Bennett, James Dunn and himself. At one time three of them studied in the same small law office in Chatham, N.B.
For more than 30 years his benefactions to his native province were many, especially in the fields of education and the performing arts. Recently he built in the city of Fredericton a new theatre, which has not yet been officially opened. Hon. members will, of course, be aware of the Beaverbrook art gallery which he established. Lord Beaverbrook was especially interested in the field of education for more than 35 years, during which
time Beaverbrook scholarships helped hundreds of young men and women to better lives. I join with all other hon. members in paying tribute to the memory of this great man.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
As a
former professor at the University of New Brunswick who knew and appreciate the benefactions of Lord Beaverbrook, and as one whose ancestors were, a long way back, those of Lord Beaverbrook-I remember talking to him a number of years ago and he said that at one election campaign some of his political opponents said that this man's forebears were poor peasants from the isles of Mull and Ulva-so were mine-I should like to join in the tribute being paid today.
I should like to say, as an educationist, how much all of us who are interested in education appreciate what Lord Beaverbrook did himself in this field, and how by his example he prompted other men of largesse to do the same for all good causes, the first of which was education. I join with the Minister of Transport and my hon. friend from York-Sunbury in mourning today a great Canadian who was always prepared to support great causes vigorously, effectively and courageously, whether they were popular or not. I should like to add my voice to those of the two members of the house who have preceded me in expressing my regret at the loss of a great Canadian, a great friend of scholarship and, above all, a great friend of the maritimes.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
The; members of this party would like to associate themselves with those who have paid tribute to the late Lord Beaverbrook. He was a man who made a great impact on the business life of Canada and upon the world of journalism in the United Kingdom. It is to his credit that he never lost his interest in Canada and that he spent much of his wealth in furthering education and learning in the province of New Brunswick, where his heart always remained.
He leaves behind him a recollection in the minds of all who knew of him of a man whose colourful and flamboyant career in the field of journalism left an indelible mark on that

Tribute to Lord Beaverbrook profession. We join with those who have spoken in extending our deepest sympathy to his family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF EMINENT CANADIAN
speechtext:
I join with other members of this house who have spoken regarding the passing of Lord Beaverbrook.
He was a man dedicated to his convictions, courageous and charitable in a truly Canadian way; a man who was not always right, but a man brave enough to fight for what he thought to be right.
As one who knew him as a personal friend, I count his passing as a great loss. It is, indeed, a loss to Canada, to the commonwealth and to the world which will surely not soon be forgotten.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a native son of Newcastle, New Brunswick; as one who studied law in the same office to which reference has been made, in Chatham, New Brunswick, and in fact used the same desk and the same chair; as one who entered the university on a Max Aitken scholarship before there was a Lord Beaverbrook; as one who received a cablegram from his lordship within the last 72 hours expressing appreciation for a message I sent him on his birthday, I would like to associate myself with other hon. members of the house in their tributes to this great Canadian.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Yesterday I raised the question of the treatment of a Greek seaman, Mr. Thomadakis. I should like to ask the minister how he can square his statement yesterday that Mr. Thomadakis was informed of his right to be represented by a lawyer and that Thomadakis was satisfied with the qualifications of the interpreter who works for the department, with Mr. Thomadakis' habeas corpus application filed with the Ontario supreme court in which he states:
On April 9, 1964 I got a letter saying I would go to court next day. I had not a chance to get in touch with anyone as the letter came in afternoon and jail regulations say I must put in requests in the morning.
Mr. Thomadakis' application further states:
No one told about legal aid....I went to court on April 10 (38 days after my arrest) for the first time. I had no lawyer and interpreter for immigration told me to plead guilty and I go home. If I make trouble and plead not guilty I go back to jail until the case comes up again and maybe I get a heavy prison sentence.

Inquiries of the Ministry
This is a pretty serious allegation. I wonder whether the minister can make any statement on it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the case is now before the court. Moreover, I think that the allegations just made by the hon. member are part of a document which has just been submitted to an Ontario court. I wonder if it would be in order for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to comment on that matter at this stage of the proceedings.

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: Order. I should like to explain to the house that the hon. member came to my office this morning to discuss this question. I thought it was a very serious matter in principle and that if he would ask a question, even if it was slightly longer than usual, he would be justified in the circumstances rather than trying to adjourn the house under standing order 26 or raising a question of privilege.

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister this question. If he feels he cannot make a public statement, will he at least investigate what kind of advice Mr. Thomadakis was given by the interpreter, and whether he was in fact informed that he could get free legal aid?

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made a statement in the house about this and I think the answer was given at that time.

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. When the minister is looking into this particular case will he also look at the much wider question which has been raised by legal aid lawyer Allan Mintz, who has made the statement that he visited the Don jail and that he finds there are 20 prisoners there, all of whom have informed him they were never told at any time that they were entitled to legal counsel? subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed by officials of my department that, in every case, detained persons were told that they could secure legal counsel to present their case.

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS
subsubtopic: LEGAL COUNSEL
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would the minister consider the suggestion made the last time we discussed this matter and which we make again today, that he arrange to have inquiries made about this very serious matter by people outside of his department, who can be somewhat more impartial than the officials who are involved in these cases?

subtopic: JOHN THOMADAKIS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understood that another member adjourned the debate the last time this matter was before the house. However, if he is not prepared to speak at this time I should like to say a few words. There seems to be a feeling that bills have to be passed in a hurry for fear that one may be accused of holding up legislation. However, with the record set by the government of introducing legislation and having to withdraw some of it after scrutiny, I feel I should say a few words at this time.
My first words are of commendation of the farm credit advisers within the department. They have done a fine job with the existing legislation. In the last year some 21,000 would-be applicants consulted with the advisers. Of these some 9,800 completed the forms. Some 3,000 did not complete the forms, but they were either ineligible or were merely seeking some advice in respect of financing. This in itself is an invaluable service to the farming community.
In the few years that the Farm Credit Corporation have been in existence they have made a substantial number of loans. In 195960 there were 5,339 loans made. There were 5,597 loans made in 1960-61, 5,885 in 196162, 7,438 in 1962-63 and 8,689 in 1963-64. This indicates that there is increasing interest in the availability of loans to farmers. But what is remarkable is that of some 24,000 loans that have been made in the last five years, only eight properties are at present being held by the corporation. This in itself speaks very highly for the farm credit advisers and for the farmers who have obtained these loans.
In the fiscal year 1962-63 some 94.3 per cent of the loans were in good standing. It is understandable that there may perhaps be certain cases where the payments could not be made at the required time because of circumstances that may have arisen. However, a record of that type should commend
Farm Credit Act
itself to the house. It arises out of the fact that the legislation makes it quite easy for farmers to repay their loans, and at the same time the legislation performs a great service for the farming community.
As I listened to the Minister of Agriculture when he introduced the bill on June 2, I noted that he said there was some $22 million still available in the fund. This is running fairly close to the line. He also indicated that loans were being made at the rate of about $1 million per day. It would seem, therefore, that as of today there should be some $14 million available in the fund. To me this is reminiscent of the Easter recess that never was, because a similar situation arose with regard to the unemployment insurance fund. In the rush to get the legislation through at that time the government wanted the opposition to close its eyes to some of the weaknesses inherent in the legislation and in the organization and operation of the unemployment insurance fund at the present time.
It is interesting to note that this is the first legislation the Minister of Agriculture may hope to have passd by the house. I can recall other days when one of the suggestions made by those who form the government today was that bold and imaginative legislation would be forthcoming. I fail to see that there is anything of that nature in this instance when the government waits until a few days before the deadline and then introduces legislation in the hope that no opposition members will speak for fear they will be criticized on the ground that they are holding up legislation. I fail to see that there is any imagination when all the minister is doing is doubling the amount of money available in the fund. Not only is he doubling the amount of the fund; he is also increasing the interest rate under this legislation.
I would have thought that the minister would have come forth with something revolutionary, something new, something that the farmers did not even expect from the government. However, he has to rely on amending a piece of legislation that was introduced in 1959. Because it was a new venture in farm credit at that time, naturally certain things came up which could not have been foreseen. Amendments were introduced in 1962. Because the minister now finds himself short of funds and because he wants to make it appear that he is really doing something for the farming community, he introduces an amendment to double the

Farm Credit Act
amount of money available in the fund and then claims that he is really doing something for the farmers.
While many may express the hope that this legislation will do a lot for the farming community, I fail to see it from that point of view. My point of view may differ from that of some who have already spoken, but I feel I should point out certain things that will arise as a result of this type of legislation. I have always been one who has believed that credit is essential. Having used it myself, I am a believer that it can be helpful to the farming community. However, one can reach the point of diminishing return.

It will be noted that according to the 1961 census report there were some 480,000 farms in Canada. There were some 430,000 of these farms with acreages of less than 750 acres. In fact, there were 400,000 farms with acreages of less than 550 acres. Now we come to the average capitalization of farms of 750 acres or less and we find that the average capitalization was $37,000. The minister is increasing the availability of funds by making loans in the order of $40,000 to $55,000 available. If one takes into account the fact that a loan may not exceed 75 per cent of the appraised value, he finds that a farmer will have to have to farm with a capital value of at least $50,000 to $60,000 to take advantage of these amendments. According to the 1961 census table, farms with an average capital value of $61,000 contain 1,120 acres to 1,600 acres. I suggest to the minister that despite the fact he may wish to

Farm Credit Act
say he is doing a lot for the farmers, I am suggesting that he may be doing something for those farmers in the higher income group, but he is not really helping out the ones who are in difficulty at the moment. The minister may be able to produce statistics in a few years which will indicate that the average farm income has gone up as a result of an increase in the number of these bigger farms, because the cost of production on these farms will naturally be far less than the cost of production of the average smaller farmer.
However, the minister has not yet solved the problem of the average farmer. It is interesting to note, as I said earlier, that there are some 400,000 farms with less than 550 acres. The average capital value per farm of less than 500 acres was $30,000. At the moment there are provisions making loans available to this type of farmer. I repeat that the minister, in introducing this legislation, is not helping the small farmer. There may be specific types of agriculture that might require this type of legislation. However, I do not want the minister saying in the future that he is doing something for everybody. I think we will find that there will be specialized farm groups who will perhaps require this type of loan. I do not want the minister expanding it to include everybody.
One other thing we will have to guard against in the future is the fact that these larger farms are going to be incorporated. In the last few years, we have heard a considerable amount about vertical integration. I point out that according to the poultry market report for June 5, the price of eggs in Saskatchewan on May 30, 1964, was 14.8 cents per dozen. Why were these eggs sold at this price? It is for the simple reason that some farmers who have gone into egg production in a big way have over-produced, and the end result is that the smaller farmers cannot compete against these bigger producers.
In the field of turkey production those with capital available and who are already established have also gone into it in a big way. I can point to many farmers in my constituency, as I am sure other hon. members can in theirs, who have had up to 1,000 turkeys. If they got $5 per turkey this gave them $5,000 at the end of the year, but this was not $5,000 profit. They had to depend on the sale of their eggs, wheat and other produce to make an adequate living for their families.
Credit may now become available to establish these large farms which the minister has been used to, and which in his experience

he has found to be profitable operations. If a farmer has 60,000 turkeys and makes 25 cents on each turkey, he has $15,000 profit, but the return to a man with less than a thousand turkeys is $250, which is very little. He has to have additional income. The minister and the farm credit advisers must take this fact into account when they are making this credit available, so that we will not end up with a group of land barons, a select few owning all land while all the rest have to work for them.
If the minister does this, then he will create another problem. There will be a greater demand for unemployment insurance to be paid to these people, something which the government is not prepared to pay now. The Gill commission did not recommend it. If the government is not prepared to subsidize agricultural produce it will have to take other measures such as providing unemployment insurance. I hope the minister will take note of these remarks because I feel very strongly about this thing.
Another problem which I feel will arise is that land values will increase. If this happens, then those who are already established on economic units will be able to outbid those others who would like to establish themselves on economic units. In other words, they will be quite prepared to take a lower return per unit than those seeking to make their present units economical, and these smaller operators will be forced out of farming.
A practice has been established whereby, for example, if a man wants to purchase land valued at $10,000, the Farm Credit Corporation is prepared to give him the money, but if he makes a deal for land valued at $15,000 he has to put up $5,000 of his own. It is unreasonable to expect a small operator to be able to put up $5,000. The larger operator will, and he will outbid the small farmer who will be driven out of the business; and if he is driven out of the business the government will have to provide a subsidy for him in some other form.
There will have to be a complete review of all existing farm legislation. One point that bothers me is the 5 per cent provision on loans up to $20,000 under part II, and loans up to $27,500 under part III. This is one of the stipulations we fought for and placed on the statute books because we felt it was a fair amount to charge.
You will find that over the years the interest rate will fluctuate, and the amount the corporation might be expected to lose,

while it might appear great at the moment, if interest rates go down will not be so great, and in the end will balance up. Now, under the proposed amendment, the charges will be-
-an amount equal to the cost of the corporation of any money borrowed for the purposes of the loan and the expenses of the corporation in respect thereof, including a reasonable reserve against loss.
There are two reasons why I would object to this. I feel this may be a deterrent to small farmers, and I feel that any person who finds it necessary to take a loan of over $20,000 under the new provisions, or over $27,500, may have to carry in his interest charges sufficient for all the losses which may be incurred with respect to loans that were formerly made up to $20,000 and up to $27,500.
If $10 million in loans were outstanding, in order to recover this amount in some cases you would have to charge up to a rate of 10 per cent, and it is estimated that $1 million is lost every year under the provisions as they exist now. If as I believe only 10 per cent of the farmers will be in a position to borrow over $27,500, and if they are to make good this loss, you will have to charge them a rate of over 10 per cent.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I wish to clarify one thing so that I might not persist unduly, if that were not the case.
There is another problem which arises. Apparently, the minister hopes to get the corporation into a position where it will suffer no losses. However, there will still be a loss. If I am correct in assuming that only 10 per cent of the people affected will take loans over and above the amount presently available, there could conceivably be added another 10 per cent to the $1 million presently being lost by the corporation. This, in itself, would amount to $100,000. It seems that to recover a loss of $100,000 we go to a lot of trouble. But this, in itself, is not the point. If the minister feels the royal commission on banking and finance has recommended such action, and it is essential, he may be relying on this recommendation to strengthen his argument. But I say that if this is a first step toward a move which will unjustly penalize farmers, it cannot be supported. I am afraid the minister will say that if interest is not being charged at 74 per cent, or 7 per cent, or anything above 5 per cent we will lose money. And in a few years he will suggest to the house again that we should withdraw the 5 per cent provision and charge according to the rate which the corporation must pay in order to get it.
I suggest strongly, for this reason, that a first step should not be taken in this direction. I do not want the minister to say at a later date: We have found out we do not have to lose money on the Farm Credit Corporation. The commission on banking and finance told us what was the practice to be followed. If we continue to do this we shall find ourselves in another awkward situation. Someone will want a loan, and will be charged 7 or 8 per cent. In a few years we shall be able to borrow money for less than that. As the minister well knows, interest rates have gone up-from 4J to 5 per cent to 54 per cent and so on. If a farmer has agreed to pay interest at 7 per cent and then finds the corporation is able to lend him the money at a lower rate of interest he should be able to recover the amount he is overpaying. I think provision should be made for this, and I do not see any such provision in the bill before us enabling a farmer to recover any funds to which he may rightly be entitled.

Farm Credit Act
I see my time is running out, but there is one other matter with which I should like to deal briefly. It appears there were some 77,000 farm improvement loans taken out last year while there were 8,000 which might be considered long term loans. I think the minister will have to introduce legislation to make provision for an increase in farm improvement loans, because this is an area where I feel availability of credit can do far more good than action in other directions which might tend to create land barons at the expense of small farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not an expert in agricultural matters and I will not speak about them very long either.
I wanted to add to the reason you gave for preventing the minister from answering questions addressed to him the fact that he does not occupy his seat now, thus being forbidden to speak. If you examine Bill No. C-100, you will find that beekeeping has been added to the special agricultural fields, which will enable beekeepers to take advantage of the Farm Credit Act.
I am very pleased with this amendment because there are in my riding some well-known beekeepers, and I am convinced that they will be happy to find that they can benefit from the advantages offered by the Farm Credit Act.
As far as the increase in the amounts specified by the legislation is concerned, I believe that the minister tried to sit on the agricultural fence. That is good, very commendable to try it, but I believe that in increasing the amount of the loans, we want to help those who, in theory, should be well off since we include them among the most prosperous farmers. While helping them, at the same time we tell them: You have enough money to pay the additional interest. Therefore, we will lend you the $27,500 and we will charge you for the cost of the loan.
This means that the Farm Credit Act would be no longer a legislation intended to assist the farmers, but simply a measure replacing the banks and other finance companies.
In my opinion, the government should not substitute itself for the banks in such cases. The purpose of the act is to help farmers and if it is felt that farmers who need as much as $40,000 or $55,000 should be helped because they are not rich, then the rate of interest on their loans should not exceed 5

per cent. On the other hand, if some farmers are rich enough to pay more than 5 per cent interest, they should not be allowed to borrow as much as that under the act.
One of the recommendations of the Porter commission on banking deals with the removal of the maximum rate of interest applicable to bank loans so that banks may raise their rates. If an individual borrowed more than $27,500 because he thinks he will be charged about 6 per cent interest on the amount outstanding and if that recommendation of the Porter commission is acted upon by the government, the borrower will find that he is actually paying 10, 12 and 15 per cent interest.
I submit that this provision can lead to difficulties and I would ask the minister to give it full consideration before putting it into practice.

speechtext:
I know many people will be very interested in the bill now before us which contains provision for increasing the amount of money which can be made available under the act. However I think there are many who begin to wonder if credit is really being considered in terms of assuring the agricultural future of our nation.
Canada is of course a young nation, and I presume we have much to learn from what has been done elsewhere. In the last 40 or 50 years a problem has been facing other countries which is not dissimilar to that which faces Canada. In Great Britain, over the years, it was felt that the democracy of the nation hinged on the English countryside. However, as the small farms disappeared over the years, democracy was considered to be no less prevalent in that country. France, on the other hand, went to the other extreme. Larger and larger farm units were developed in that country, as we are developing them in Canada, until there was a very large and easily controlled agricultural population. It could also be said that by developing themselves on a family farm scale they were in the process, because of government control, of losing real democracy in the agricultural field.
The United States has also been concerned with this subject and it is interesting to note in a book "Farming and Democracy" by Griswold that the author, speaking of the Truman economic report, states:
Thus, it completed the definition of a policy that had begun with farmers in general and ended with farmers in particular, that in the beginning

had taken the family farm for granted and in the end had made it a specific item of national interest. On this high level it was incorporated in President Truman's economic report of 1947.
The cycle of policy thus concluded sets the United States apart from both England and France. It shows a national concern for agriculture as a state of society, for private property in land, and for family farming as their mainstay, that has simply not existed in England-a concern that played little part in the development of British democracy and almost throttled its development in France.
He goes on to say:
The British experience shows us that it is possible to reduce the farm population to an irreducible minimum, and small, owner-operated family-size farms virtually to extinction, and still have democracy. The French contrast shows us that it is possible to maintain a maximum farm population and carry family farming to its extreme logical conclusion, and all but lose democracy in the bargain.
I believe it is very simple to change the rules and regulations of farm credit, but I think the government certainly has some responsibility in deciding what is to be the basis of agriculture in Canada and just what we are trying to work toward. I believe that the agricultural development of Canada, which is extensive and has been the mainstay of our economy for many years and has probably been the basis of our development, has been and has to be in the future a partnership of three large groups, the farmer and the rural community, the markets and the marketing agencies and their operations, and government itself, because government policies play a great role in where agriculture is going. One might ask why we should discuss this when we are deciding on the extension of credit, but it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if we are not willing to take a look at it we are being very unfair to agriculture and we may in effect bankrupt it.
I would like to give an example, Mr. Speaker. If tomorrow a car manufacturer was able to find a credit agency that would grant credit on a new car on a ten year basis, you might think this was a very reasonable way of buying that car. But if you were doing very much travelling as a salesman or in many other fields, you would find the profitable lifetime of that car to be probably only three years. So during the last seven years of the loan you would be paying for a car that had long disappeared, and the problem would arise at least twice following that situation. This applies to farmers in particular. I am sure there are dairy farmers today who, knowing the changes the minister has made in agriculture, will be worried about whether some of the commodities they are
Farm Credit Act
producing have remained economic. If the government is going to lend this large amount of money to a farmer in order that he may develop an economic farm unit, the government also has an obligation to take some action in the marketplace and in the direction of the national economy in order to provide some protection for the farmer to whom they have lent money to set up an economic farm unit; that is to say, protection so that this economic farm unit will not be destroyed by their allowance of change in these other two fields.
I suggest this has already happened in vertical integration. The farmer was given an unlimited amount of credit; he was given so much credit that it was only a matter of a year or two before he lost the farm, and in many cases these farms are no longer in operation. This was repeated in the field of poultry farming, in the production of pork, and it has been repeated in regard to many other crops, such as potatoes and, I understand, tobacco in some areas. So vertical integration provided a very large amount of money, too large an amount of money to be economical for the operation and the maintenance of the farm for the farmer who borrowed the money. The government has responsibilities in the field of crop failure which may be general or local. It has a responsibility when it withdraws support prices for a particular commodity, and it has a responsibility when a change takes place in the rural aid development programs. Each of these have a reflection on the ability of the unit to remain an economic farm unit and each makes all the difference between whether or not the borrower of the money under farm credit is able to make a success of his venture.
It seems to me that if the government, the market place and the farmers are not brought together and the matter discussed, a problem is going to develop with regard to many of these farmers that has not been contemplated.
I also read further from this book called "Farming and Democracy". This relates to an incident which took place when the small, non-economic units were being removed to make way for progress, and much more suitable economic units. The book quotes the famous colloquy between one of Steinbeck's Okies and a tractor driver whom he has threatened to shoot for knocking over his buildings and plowing up his land and shows the direction, if not the precise location, in which the blame lies. The conversation is quoted in this way:
"It's not me. There's nothing I can do."

Farm Credit Act
This is the tractor driver talking:
"I'll lose my job if I don't do it.-And look- suppose you kill me? They'll just hang you, but long before you're hung there'll be another guy on the tractor, and he'll bump the house down. You're not killing the right guy".
"That's so", the tenant said. "Who gave you orders? I'll go after him. He's the one to kill".
"You're wrong. He got his orders from the bank. The bank told him-'Clear those people out or it's your job' ".
"Well, there's a president of the bank. There's a board of directors. I'll fill up the magazine of the rifle and go into the bank".
The driver said, "Fellow was telling me the bank gets orders from the east. The orders were, 'Make the land show profit or we'll close you up' ".
"But where does it stop? Who can we shoot...?"
The Okie could not shoot the industrial revolution. He could not shoot our failure to devise a public policy that would put that revolution to the advantage of our whole population. But he could, and did, testify to the fact that, in his case, and the cases of a million or more of his fellows, agriculture by itself had performed no democratic miracles.
The previous speaker mentioned the fact that this may do just what the tractor driver was going to do to the Okie's shack; it may eliminate many of the small farms in the community as increased loans are provided. It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that in order to do something about this the minister should suggest that supervisory boards be set up that are, again, made up of three parts: government policy, represented by government representation; the farm problem, represented by the rural agricultural groups, federations, farmers' unions, and so on; and the market place has to be represented, because unless the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is going to sell the products we manufacture, we are dependant upon our domestic market, with its rapid fluctuations.
I know that increasing the amount of money that can be borrowed is a very easy way for the minister to make himself popular, and it is probably an easy way for me, speaking in opposing it, to make myself unpopular. I am not really opposing it, because I am sure there is a certain merit in classified cases; but it is very easy to go out and offer somebody a lot of money. Household Finance is doing it every day successfully, at a very high rate of interest, and the people who are borrowing this money know that by doing so they are just putting themselves further into debt.
I think we should guide some of the thinking in this regard. I refer to not only the thinking between the farmer and the advisory board that we now have, but be-

tween the agriculturists of Canada and the government, in terms of what we want agriculture to provide Canada.
It is all very nice for us to say, "Maintain the family farm", but this is not maintaining the family farm. A $55,000 loan means a repayment, at the end of 30 years, of well over $125,000; that is what a person will have to pay back. If you look at the statistics for Canada and the amount of money being received in the way of farm income, you will understand that this type of loan will be limited to very few people on an economic basis. Therefore this is not a general policy; it is not going to apply to too many people. The previous speaker also mentioned that 87 per cent of the people receive less than $20,000 in loans; that this was a very satisfactory arrangement for many people. I am not suggesting there should be no extension but I think the government must take some responsibility to provide a loan for those who want it.
I am sure everyone is aware that many of the farmers who want to operate an economic farm unit today, perhaps in the $40,000 or $50,000 class, will not be able to operate that unit, if we provide them with enough money to make the expansion allowed under the terms of this act, unless as an agency we are willing to provide them with managerial training to handle such a large business. Everyone is aware that some small businesses in a small town operate successfully until the boss becomes unaware of the names of his employees and of what is going on. I did some negotiating with one company, and the boss said to me that he did not trust the accountants or any of the people working for him, because he asked them for an inventory check and was told that there were no parts in stock which were not included in the inventory. Yet he told me that he could produce some parts not in the inventory at all. Therefore, in an expansion of this kind one requires managerial training, which I am sure many farmers have not had.
We are not being fair to many of these people, if as a national policy we try to increase the size of the farms to provide a more healthy agricultural economy, unless we provide this type of training; and the government shirks its responsibility in this as in many other fields. An agricultural unit of $100,000 or $150,000 could be made completely uneconomical if tomorrow the government increased the tariff on farm machinery and the farmer had to pay 30 to 35 per cent more on the cost of a combine. If

the farmer has economically geared his operation to the costs of today, then obviously the government will play an increasing role in what he does. But we must try to meet rural sociological problems and provide solutions for them.
In offering the farmers more money we are creating a hazard in many areas. I am sure that the government receives more requests for money from people in the lower income groups than from those in the higher income groups. It may not be a good thing, but it it true that some farmers seem to get along with a reported income of $1,000. The majority of farmers in many areas are reporting incomes to the income tax department of around that amount. If that is so, and if these units appear to provide the basis of our rural economy in many areas, I suggest that that minister take a look at the other extreme in considering this matter of credit, and gives some of the farmers in my area who are asking for $2,000 or $3,000 a little more consideration. There is a kind of grand and glorious attitude on the part of many officials that if a farmer wants the maximum they will consider it; but if a farmer is interested in only a minimum amount he obviously has an uneconomical farm unit. I believe there are considerations at both ends of the picture. We want to expand the economic farm unit, and in many areas that unit is some 160 acres whereas in others it is 320. There are many places in western Canada where a unit would not be considered economical unless it exceeded a section of land. Many of my farm friends in western Canada have said that if a unit is not at least three sections it is not sufficiently large enough to carry the capital expenditure for the type of equipment they have on their farms.
The sociological change in rural Canada is a factor in the decision to grant and extend credit. I believe the government has completely failed to give guidance and leadership in this field. It has been said that to grant a large sum of money only means the extension of the principle of vertical integration; that one farmer who has proved competent to have his farm paid up will have enough land to enable him to borrow the maximum amount from the government, and this will enable him to squeeze out all his neighbours because he can outbid them in the marketplace as a result of the money he borrowed under the act. This creates a social problem which the government has a responsibility to meet.
Farm Credit Act
I imagine that the minister has not enough knowledge of the whole subject to understand this particular problem. I imagine it has been very hard for him even to understand some of the problems put to him which contradict the principle of extending credit, particularly at the lower end of the scale. But there are those in the universities of Canada, as there have been in the United States, who have been appointed to commissions to study the problem and have made recommendations not in keeping with the recommendations now being made regarding the extension of large amounts of credit. The Canadian Senate over the years has discussed land use problems and the maintenance of our rural economy. Representations have also been made by other bodies, including this house, to the effect that owing to the distribution of seats this house had a predominantly rural representation. Yet I wonder whether many rural representatives have really considered what the extension of those large amounts of credit has meant to the rural communities. The farm communities themselves are tending to disappear, and in some areas just one or two farmers own a whole township. People nowadays prefer to sell ice cream along the highway on Sundays rather than general hardware, groceries and other commodities in a rural oriented economy.
It is easy for the Liberal party, as was the case in the last election, to offer to extend credit to every Tom, Dick and Harry whether or not it would be of any value to them, to the community or to the nation. But I believe the minister has an obligation to bring in legislation to relate the total development of rural Canada to the credit needs of the nation so that we do not continue to give credit to those who do not really need it, such as the type of person who could put up his own collateral at the bank. We should give more consideration to the little farmer on the back concession who only wants a couple of thousand dollars to buy the farm across the road. It may not be an economical farm unit, but it has probably supported his father and his grandfather, as well as providing for the education of three or four generations of Canadians, and with a small expansion will be able to continue to support a family for some years to come. In my experience very little consideration has been given to this aspect of farm credit.
It seems to me that this is one of the areas in which the Farm Credit Corporation has

Farm Credit Act
failed to function to advantage. Some farmers with managerial ability will be able to take advantage of the increase in the maximum amount of loans to $55,000. There are many farmers who, before they borrow $55,000, would be well advised to think about retiring the debt in an organized manner, because I am aware of the fact that without supervision, without the support of a government that is prepared to look 30 years ahead, many of those who will borrow larger sums of money from the Farm Credit Corporation will find themselves in difficulty.
Those who do not realize the vast change in agriculture that will take place in the next few years need only look back 30 years when almost all agricultural work was done with horses. Today the horse is an oddity that is shown at agricultural fairs throughout rural Canada through grants being made to entrepreneurs in other fields to maintain the heavy draft horse breed. I think this indicates the changes that have taken place and it is prophetic of the changes that will take place in the future. Unless the government is now prepared to make known an agricultural policy that will make it clear what the government hopes to get out of agriculture in Canada and what the future for agriculture will be, I and many farmers will interpret the increase in the maximum amount of loan, together with the fact that the minister has tied with this an interest rate in keeping with the full costs rather than the original rate of 5 per cent, to be a trend in the development of rural Canada that is not designed to maintain the family farm and the family farm unit.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a very few questions that I wish to ask the minister arising out of his speech on June 2. I know he cannot answer them right away but I would appreciate it if he would take note of the questions on which I seek clarification and answer them when he closes the debate.
First of all I should like to compliment the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation and his staff upon the excellent work they have done. I can speak from personal knowledge of the officials in my own area. I think they have done a marvellous job, and I think the house will agree that any advancement in the administration of this program must be brought about by means of changes in the act. I am very pleased to see that the minister has taken these requirements into consideration.

In the minister's speech the other day he made reference to an economic unit. I should like him to define what he means by an economic unit, and indicate how it is determined. I should also like him to relate that to the reference he made to a family farm. Are an economic unit and the family farm the same thing? I would also ask the minister to say a few words with regard to whether he has given any consideration to the idea that loans should be based on the ability and record of the applicant. At the present time they are based on the security of land. I suggest to the minister that the aspect of security could be covered by the applicant taking out life insurance.
At the present time we find that the difficulty with the Canadian Farm Loan Act is that the present high market value and the conservative agricultural production value reduce the number of qualifying farmers considerably, and to obtain the maximum amount of loan requires a fairly large unit. A farmer operating a large farm cannot obtain a loan, since he already owns what the officials consider is an economic unit, and the smaller farmer cannot obtain a loan large enough to purchase even a quarter section since he has not sufficient land.
I understand that Ontario has had a scheme for a number of years under which a young farmer can apply for a loan from the provincial government. His application is then referred to a board consisting of his neighbours or the municipal authorities in that locality to determine whether this man will be a good risk, and on the basis of their recommendation he is allowed to obtain a loan. I also understand that under this system there have been very few losses in the province of Ontario.
The difficulty that members of parliament encounter with regard to loans from the Farm Credit Corporation is that the officials are hamstrung by the restrictions in the act. This issue has come up time and time again. However, most members know that these applicants are conscientious people with good farming records, but because of the lack of capital they do not have what is considered to be an economic unit. I refer again to that term, "economic unit", because it seems to vary according to localities.
I was very interested in what the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) had to say with regard to interest rates. To my mind the proposal in the amendment to the act is discriminatory. I say this because the minister has not actually laid out what the interest

rate can be. As I read the legislation it can be based on three different qualifications. It is set forth that the rate will not be more than the interest charged to the corporation, plus the cost of administration and a reasonable reserve against loss. That could vary anywhere from 6 per cent up to 8 or 9 per cent, and that is why I say this provision is discriminatory.
If it is necessary to increase the rate from 5 per cent I think it would be more advisable to set out the rate in the bill. Then there would be no danger of one farmer taking a loan this year and because of these three factors having to pay 8 per cent, and another farmer taking a loan next year and finding that a rate of 6J per cent will cover the loan on the basis of a period of 30 years.
I should also like to ask the minister what he means when he refers to the interest rate as an economic rate. That is a very elastic phrase. As I said before, economic farm units can vary from locality to locality. Would the same rate apply to loans in Ontario and loans in Saskatchewan? Would there be a different interest rate?
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: SEICHO-NO-IE
SEICHO-NO-IE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-23, to incorporate Seicho-No-Ie.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. S-23 is somewhat unusual in that it seeks to incorporate a religious body of Japanese origin. For that reason my explanation may take a little longer than would otherwise be the case. The religious movement from which this religious body emanated was known as Seicho-No-Ie and was founded in 1930 by Dr. Masaharu Taniguchi, who lived at that time in the town of Sumiyoshi, Japan. Taniguchi was a scholar who was born in Kobe, Japan in 1893. He majored in English literature at Waseda university in Tokyo. When he started Seicho-No-Ie, he was a translator for a subsidiary of an American oil company in Japan.
He was a student of many religious philosophies. It was his aim to seek the truth where-ever it may be found. He named the religious body that he founded Seicho-No-Ie, which
Private Bills
means in English, "The home of spiritual growth and prosperity" and is sometimes also referred to as "The house of life, wisdom and abundance."
This Bill No. S-23, is in the usual form of a bill incorporating a religious body. It is the first incorporation by the parliament of Canada of a religious body having its origin in Japan. However, there is a precedent for the incorporation of a religious body from another area of the world. In 1949, the parliament of Canada passed a bill which is now chapter 25 of the statutes of that year, to incorporate The National Spiritual Assembly of the Baha'is of Canada. This bill was assented to on April 30, 1949.
This organization has a membership of two million people, although it should be noted that all of its members are free to belong to other religious faiths as well, and many do. Japanese religious ideas are somewhat different from those prevailing in Christian countries and one is not tied down in the matter of membership, as is the custom in Canada. Originally, the founder, Taniguchi, was more interested in proclaiming his religious and philosophical ideas rather than in setting up a religious system as such. He started out first by publishing a monthly magazine that he called Seicho-No-Ie.
Taniguchi was influenced by Mary Baker Eddy, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Ernest Holmes and other writers of that group, and he acknowledges openly his debt to them. His ideas on religion resemble the ideas of Christian Science and of the unity school of Christianity. He has, however, made a very distinct contribution to Japanese religious thought by introducing Christian ideas developed in the nineteenth century in the United States into Japan in a form that proved acceptable to Buddhists, Shintoists and other Japanese who would not normally be inclined to subscribe to foreign religious ideas.
In order to get his ideas across to the Japanese public, in addition to this monthly magazine, Taniguchi encouraged visitors to come to his home to consult with him. Eventually he set up regular subscribers meetings, as he called them, in his own home. He then proceeded to give lectures in various centres at the request of people who were sympathetic to his ideas. He developed a form of meditation called Shinsookan, which might be described as a form of prayerful meditation, with the purpose of bringing the individual consciousness of the practitioner in contact with the absolute. The members of this organization regard this approach to religion as

Private Bills
analogous to the approach of the mystics of medieval Christianity. This is the way they look at it.
Taniguchi has written several religious poems which may be recited in approximately 20 minutes to half an hour. These have come to be used as texts for common recitation in the study groups and subscribers groups of the religious body. These poems actually summarize Taniguchi's doctrinal position.
Within five or six years after he started his organization Taniguchi added another magazine which was meant more entirely for women, and in a few years more he added a magazine edited for children and for people who were incapable of understanding very difficult Japanese. He also added a magazine for educators, and another which has a strong philosophical orientation.
He has always welcomed people from other religious groups and assured them that they do not have to sever their connections with their family religions. In fact, he has persuaded them to continue holding their funeral and marriage services in the religions to which they belonged before joining his group. In order to get away from the traditional religious atmosphere of Japanese religions, he refused to call his congregation churches, temples or shrines. Instead, he talked about subscriber groups, fellowship groups and branches. As this religious movement grew, he eventually transferred its headquarters to Tokyo.
The leaders of groups are called lecturers, not ministers, priests or anything that would remind one of traditional churches. He was at all times trying to emphasize content rather than form. However, the Japanese ministry of education was at a loss as to how it should consider or treat this organization for administration purposes, and eventually his organization was persuaded to register as a religious body in Japan. Today it is so registered, and it includes shrines within its branches. It accepts donations and it operates as a religious organization in Japan. It is recognized as such, although its earlier spirit of emphasizing content rather than outer form has remained.
Dr. Taniguchi is referred to as the president of the organization. The affairs of the organization are managed by a board of directors, under his chairmanship. The Tokyo head office pretty well controls the entire religious activities which are carried out in Japan, Brazil, Peru, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Sweden and Canada. There are approximately 1,200 members in

Canada with groups in Vancouver, New Westminster, Richmond, Slocan, and Steves-ton in British Columbia, and others in Hamilton, Montreal and Toronto. The organization is incorporated in California, Japan, Hawaii, Brazil and Mexico. Its main centre in North America is Los Angeles. Its head office, as you will see from section 3 of the bill, will be in Toronto.
A point which will be of interest to all hon. members is that during the last war, when Japanese activities in the United States were carefully watched and controlled, the Seicho-No-Ie organization was permitted to function by the government of that country, and its books were allowed to be published and distributed in normal fashion. I believe this should be some guarantee.
The movement seeks a world of perfect harmony for all men. It is non-denominational. It neither bars nor excludes any true religion, be it Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism, Shintoism or otherwise. In a sense, it may be said to seek to be an umbrella over all true religions. It seeks a world describable as the kingdom of God on earth and endeavours to have man recognize his own perfect and divine nature, and to steep himself with the conviction that he is a child of God.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have made no great personal study of this religion, and I do not intend to go further into its teachings and characteristics. However, I should like to say that the members of this organization consist of well educated and highly respected people. Included among their members is a former prime minister of Japan, lawyers, school teachers, doctors and university professors. Personally, I believe it to be a peaceful, nonviolent and sincere religious movement and that in the spirit of the Canadian Bill of Rights it is a movement that is entitled to incorporation in this country.
I would ask that the bill be given second reading and then referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills where all members of that committee will have a good chance to ask questions and obtain more detailed answers.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PREFERENCE OF BILINGUAL APPOINTMENTS
PROVISION FOR PREFERENCE OF BILINGUAL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill

No. C-34, respecting employment of bilingual persons in the public service and in crown corporations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce Bill No. C-34 entitled:
An act respecting employment of bilingual persons in the public service and in crown corporations.
Allow me to read a few excerpts from this bill:
... it shall be the duty of the person or persons responsible for such appointments to give a preference to bilingual persons so that there shall be in the public service, in crown corporations, in works, undertakings and businesses above mentioned, a number of bilingual persons proportionate to the number of French speaking Canadians throughout the country. The purpose of this bill is to correct, in so far as it is possible to do so, the discrimination which now exists in the public service and in crown corporations in the recruiting and employment of persons of French origin, and to give a preference to bilinguists.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this bill requires that a third of the employees in all government services, including crown corporations, be bilingual.
To give you an example of the present shortage of bilingual employees in those services, allow me to quote from a brief published by the Conseil de la vie frangaise. Concerning the Department of External Affairs, the linguistic knowledge is as follows:

Mr. Speaker, the law provides that all French Canadians must be bilingual in every government department, including crown corporations. However, this provision does not apply to other elements in our country.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) promised that a bonus would be paid to bilingual civil servants. Besides, this was included in the platform of the Liberal party during the last election campaign, according to a newspaper advertisement. I am very much surprised at the position taken by the

present government in an attempt to improve the situation and to place it on a more logical basis.
I have here copies of notices of competition issued by the civil service commission of Canada.
For instance, the Department of Agriculture is looking for someone to head its information division in Ottawa; the position carries a salarly of $8,760 to $10,300. Even though the successful candidate will be working for the information division of an important department, that of agriculture, posters advertising the position do not require applicants to be bilingual.
Another competition advertised by the civil service commission concerns building construction inspectors in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Montreal and Ottawa, positions to which a salary of $6,300 to $6,960 is attached. I notice that in that case also, applicants are not required to be bilingual.
As for the competition for the position of co-ordinator of transcription, typing and reproduction services, administrative services, Department of Public Works, in Ottawa, which carries a salary of $5,760 to $6,210 candidates do not have to be bilingual. Knowledge of English is sufficient.
Another poster has to do with senior positions in nursing, public health and hospital services which command a maximum salary of $6,240 a year. Applicants will have to work in various provinces including Quebec, and yet they are not required to be bilingual.
The civil service commission has also announced a competition for foreign service stenographers for the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs. The starting salary ranges from $3,150 to $3,750 a year and, there again, applicants are not required to be bilingual.
The civil service commission also requests a head for the information service of the Department of National Revenue. Now, this head of the service must meet the requirements of the public, those of French Canada as well as those of English Canada. It was stipulated in the qualifications required of the candidates that it was essential to know both languages; but following this competition, the person who got the position is unilingual. I asked a series of questions in the house on this matter; yet, it was spelled out, in the competition notice, that candidates should have a knowledge of both languages.
I have also before me another competition notice from the civil service commission, in

Private Bills
which applications are invited for the position of "head of the editing section of another department", and there again, it is the same thing. In fact, for hours, I could list competition notices published by the civil service commission and in which it is not required that applicants have at least a knowledge of both languages. Yet, these civil servants have to work in the public interest throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, on March 5 last, in Toronto, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) lashed out at the civil service commission, which he charged with bringing about separatism among French Canadians. But I wonder what action this government means to take to remedy the present situation in the civil service commission. Reforms in this respect had been promised in order that French speaking Canadians might be on an equal footing with English speaking Canadians, as concerns civil service positions.
Mr. Speaker, at a meeting of the committee on privileges and elections, we heard some witnesses, and more particularly Mr. Keith Davey, chief organizer of the Liberal party. I asked Mr. Davey whether he received a government salary; he answered no. However, following a question I put on the order paper, as reported on pages 3354 and 3355 of Hansard for October 9, 1963, the answer given to me was that Mr. Kent was attached to the office of the Prime Minister and that his salary was $20,000 a year. We know that the Leader of the Opposition is now persistently reproving the work of the commission on bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, bilingualism is the characteristic of a country where two languages are spoken and officially recognized. Bilingualism in Canada is a fact arising out of historic circumstances; two linguistic communities have lasted side by side.
The French community has taken root in the soil of North America 350 years ago. Today, descendants of that ethnic group exceed 6 million in Canada, that is 30 per cent of the total population. They have succeeded, in spite of difficulties, in maintaining and developing the integrity of their culture. The English community settled later in Canada and it expanded through immigration from the British isles.
The English as well as the French communities have rights that are recognized under the confederation pact, which was an agreement between two provinces, but also between the two founding groups. Today, Canadians of good will are trying to find ways and means of developing within the Canadian confederation a partnership of two nationalities sharing equal rights and equal opportunities.
Every Canadian citizen has the right to speak his own language and also the right to be served in his own language by every administrative body in his country.
The Civil Service Act confirms this principle under section 47, as follows:
The number of employees appointed to serve in any department or in any local office of a department who are qualified in the knowledge and use of the English or French language or both shall, in the opinion of the commission, be sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately and to give effective service to the public.
While we are considering this bill, we reiterate the principle of French Canadian representation and we say that this representation is not, at present, what it should be as far as number and appointment to key positions are concerned. Nobody can blame French Canadians who try to improve their lot when it is a known fact that the federal government employs 334,000 persons and pays salaries amounting to $135 million a year.
The present government, through the cabinet, the Secretary of State and the Civil Service Commission of Canada is conscious of the situation and has taken immediate steps to create within the departments and the civil service, a state of mind and an awareness designed to promote a greater participation of the French element and a higher proportion of French Canadian high officials.
In order to promote bilingualism throughout Canada, the government has set up a commission to conduct a survey among the public with regard to this problem. The present government has recognized the principle of bilingualism by establishing a commission made up of an equal number of French Canadians and English Canadians, speaking both official languages. The terms of reference of this commission are specific with regard to bilingualism in the federal civil service.
May I be permitted to quote from order in council No. 1106, of July 19, 1963, the following:
-to report on the state and practice of bilingualism in all federal government services and institutions, including crown corporations, as well as in their contacts with the public, and to make recommendations to ensure the bilingual and basically bicultural character of the federal administration.
Mr. Speaker, here is a firm and resolute expression of the government's intention to respect the equal status of the founding groups of this country, and to add thereto the contribution of other ethnic groups living in Canada.
The government is building hopes on the practical findings of the Laurendeau-Dunton commission, but is adopting immediate reforms.
To permit higher level employees to learn a second language, either French or English, the civil service commission has established in Hull a bilingual school, where 460 civil servants followed a three month course. Moreover, every department offers in service courses in French and English,

Under the leadership of the Secretary of State, a cabinet committee is endeavouring to establish, on a practical level, an equal status for French and English as regards the printing of documents in every department.
To back up this cabinet committee, an interdepartmental committee composed of high officials from departments and crown corporations has been set up to bring forth concrete recommendations concerning the recruiting, the examination system, the training and promotion of personnel, to fulfil the requirements of bilingualism. To attain that objective, the government gets the full cooperation of the civil service commission and high officials.
The government is anxious to promote the recruiting of French speaking employees. The civil service commission has invited about 20 professors of the four main French speaking universities in order to give them information concerning working conditions and careers opened to university graduates.
In addition to that meeting, officials of the civil service commission go to universities and classical colleges to create interest in federal civil service jobs among the professors and students. Our French language universities and teaching institutions must increase their efforts to guide our graduates towards careers in the federal civil service. The civil service commission did make some changes in the examination procedures to take into account the Quebec education system. It must keep on playing its part by giving training and promotion opportunities to French speaking civil servants.
Mr. Speaker, there is a new determination to get a proportion of French Canadians within the federal civil service. In the present circumstances, the French speaking members of this house have to look up the civil service competition notices and encourage people to apply for these competitions by going around the teaching institutions in their riding or area, and advising their electors of the employment opportunities.
Under the leadership of our religious and civil authorities, the candidates will be more numerous and more qualified and our representation within the civil service will increase in numbers and influence.
It is the responsibility of all Canadians, from all parts of this country, to fully realize the benefits of bilingualism, to try and practice it ourselves, to encourage our young people to learn the official languages of our country, and to make known everywhere the benefits of bilingualism.

It is true that treaties, agreements, laws lay down a policy about the status of the official languages in this country, but it is above all a spirit of understanding and justice that must dictate the efforts of those who want to see the development in Canada of a spirit of greatness and unity, so that, as stated by the present Prime Minister:
All Canadians can feel confident that, within our nation, they can, protected from all discrimination and enjoying the status of full partners, build a wonderful future for them and their descendants.

Unless you live in a bilingual atmosphere in this country, acquiring the second language is very, very difficult. However, the point of the bill is that all persons in the civil service who are bilingual should receive additional pay because of this ability. With this I do not agree, and for this reason. I would suggest that where the job requires two languages, yes, they should receive additional pay. This would require a determination as to where the two languages are required. A person working in a post office in Victoria, for example, or at a border crossing point between Alberta and

Incidentally, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) for his splendid contribution as well as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) who was, himself, a distinguished bilingual official.
To ask for a proportional representation of French Canadians within the civil service regardless of competence is perhaps to venture a little too far. Of course, it must also be recognized that the civil service commission often requires for certain positions qualifications based on personal characteristics, competence and schooling of the applicant. It must be kept in mind that the Civil Service Act, as provided in chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, as well

as in regulation 21 of March 30, 1962, allows practically full discretion to the civil service commission.
I would be much more in favour of an investigation being conducted within the civil service commission as such, regardless of the matter of languages, so as to know what qualifications are required and what standards are applied before a position is given to an applicant.
There would also be the question of salaries. When we know, for instance, that someone in Quebec or in Ontario may earn $6,000, $7,000 and $8,000 in a certain position and that someone, with the same qualifications, in the maritime provinces or some of the western provinces may be satisfied with a salary of about $5,000, we realize that the Quebec candidates, who might be bilingual, may not be interested in applying for those positions. This means that it would be extremely difficult to find some empirical common ground as suggested. In my opinion, it would be necessary to study that matter in depth, rather than on the single aspect of bilingualism.
There is, for instance, in Quebec, a crown corporation whose name I shall not mention and whose English speaking employees, after attending French classes at university, are the proud holders of a certificate showing that they are proficient in the French language and therefore eligible for a salary increase or a bonus because they are bilingual. However, nothing has changed in their own attitude. They do not speak a word of French in their work and all correspondence is done by all employees in English only. Even when they do business with French Canadians who speak to them in French, they do not try to answer in French; they give negative replies or even answer in English to French Canadians.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hays for the second reading
Farm Credit Act
of Bill No. C-100, to amend the Farm Credit Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make on this bill before it is considered clause by clause in committee. At the outset, I should like to say that I welcome the amendments which have been introduced, especially the provision whereby loans under part II are to be increased to $40,000 and under part III to $55,000. There is only one reservation that I have and that is, since the interest rate is not spelled out in the bill it could mean that the interest rates charged could vary from 6 to 7 or even 8 per cent. I do not believe this is a desirable thing to have. The interest rate is set at 5 per cent in the act now. However, when the bill comes before the committee for clause by clause discussion I shall be urging the minister to make provision for a definite interest rate in these regulations.
Another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is that the definition of a farm is being broadened sufficiently to include beekeeping. I come from a province where beekeeping is a secondary industry for many farmers. In Saskatchewan we have the Saskatchewan honey co-operative which produces the so-called Sasco honey. This provision will be welcomed by the beekeepers, because they will be classified as farmers and will be eligible for loans, the same as the grain farmer or the livestock raiser.
This beekeeping industry is a very important one. In the three western provinces we have the interprovincial honey sales co-operative. It may be of interest to note that the exports of this honey amount to something like three million pounds a year, most of which goes to Britain. Since this is such a valuable source of income to the farmers, even though to some of them it may be a secondary industry, I think provision should be made in this act whereby, although a farm may not be classified strictly as a beekeeping farm and even though it is secondary to some other branch of farming such as livestock, these beekeepers should be able to obtain loans.
As I said before, this beekeeping industry is a very important one and brings in quite a bit of income. As time goes on, I am pretty sure that this interprovincial honey co-operative will expand. At the present time it is more or less the sole supplier of the market in Britain. The United Kingdom has long been

Farm Credit Act
an important market for Canadian honey and at the present time we are the exclusive suppliers of Canadian bulk honey. In my opinion, this is the appropriate time to have the beekeepers included in this clause under which they would be classified as farmers and be eligible for loans just as other farmers are.
There are many other points about which I should like to speak when we come to the clause by clause discussion. I should like to stress the fact that these loans will be increased, but since the minister will not be setting the interest rates for the loans they will not be of any help to the farmer. For instance, there might be a time when interest rates are high. After all, these loans are not taken out for only four or five years; they are taken out for 20 years or more. After some time has passed, for some unknown reason interest rates may be lower and the farmer who obtained a loan on which the interest rate is 7 per cent will be out a great deal. Therefore I urge the minister to give serious consideration to having the interest rate set the same as it is at present, namely 5 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, MAXIMUM LOAN LIMITS, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say it is now over a year since the government assumed office and we have looked forward to the presentation of legislation as an indication of the direction it would take in regard to agricultural policy. The production of any particular piece of agricultural legislation igives an indication of the direction the government is taking, and it also affects other legislation that might be brought forward from time to time.
The bill before us, if it indicates anything, indicates that the government is going for larger and larger farms, and for the ultimate elimination of the smaller farms in this country. For that reason I am deeply disturbed at the effect this legislation will have among those vast numbers of smaller farmers in my own province of Saskatchewan, farmers who have been unable to make use of the Farm Credit Corporation up to the present, and also at the effect it will have on small farmers in other areas of Canada, of whom there are great numbers in parts of the maritimes and the province of Quebec. These people at present are unable to utilize the Farm Credit Corporation under the regulations now in effect.
If I might have the minister's attention I would like to suggest to him that before the limits on the amount of loans are increased, a good long look should be taken

at the plight of those farmers who are unable to benefit from the legislation we have. These farmers are very numerous and form the bulk of the community known as the agricultural community of Canada. They have a great part to play in the orderly development of this nation in the years ahead. I do not believe the government should forget them in its haste to bring forward some legislation so that it can say it has done something with regard to agricultural problems.
Hardy farmers who at present are unable to benefit from existing legislation must know that raising the limit of loans to $55,000 is not going to mean anything to them at all. Yet these people remain the source of the greatest problems facing the nation and the Department of Agriculture.
The other matter which engages my attention is that of the interest rates, which was raised by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp).
